question: Xi Jinping out before 2027?
description:
This market will resolve to "Yes" if China's General Secretary of the Communist Party, Xi Jinping, is removed from power for any length of time between July 3, 2025, and December 31, 2026, 11:59 PM ET. Otherwise, this market will resolve to "No".

CCP General Secretary Xi Jinping will be considered removed from power if he announces his resignation from his role as General Secretary, or is otherwise dismissed, detained, disqualified, or otherwise loses his position or is prevented from fulfilling his duties as General Secretary within this market's timeframe.

The primary resolution source for this market will be a consensus of credible reporting.

eventMetadata.context_description: Xi Jinping maintains firm control over the Communist Party of China, the military, and key institutions following years of power consolidation, with no designated successor or visible internal challenges emerging ahead of the 2027 Party Congress. Recent public appearances, diplomatic engagements, and party commemorations through mid-2026 underscore his active leadership and the absence of disruptive events that might signal a transition. Traders price the “No” outcome at 95.5 percent, reflecting broad consensus that structural barriers and elite alignment make removal before 2027 highly improbable. Even so, low-probability shifts could arise from sudden health developments, unforeseen elite realignments, or major policy crises that erode support within the Politburo Standing Committee.

eventMetadata.context_description: The early stage of the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination process keeps the field open and competitive, with no major candidates having formally launched campaigns as of August 2026. Trader consensus reflects this fragmentation, assigning the highest probabilities to Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Gavin Newsom, and Jon Ossoff amid ongoing speculation over ideological balance between progressive and centrist approaches. Recent DNC decisions on the primary calendar, beginning in South Carolina, and scattered state-level polling have highlighted voter preferences without yet consolidating support behind any single contender. Ocasio-Cortez gained visibility from a University of New Hampshire survey showing her ahead in that early state, while Ossoff has drawn attention through Senate visibility and media presence. These factors sustain tight positioning among the leaders, with separation likely to emerge from midterm outcomes, formal announcements, or shifts in polling trends.
